planting.note: Sow stratified seed shallowly in fall or set out divisions in early spring along woodland edges, thickets, or partly shaded meadow margins.

directions: Sow stratified seed shallowly in fall or set out divisions in early spring along woodland edges, thickets, or partly shaded meadow margins where this rhizomatous sunflower can spread into loose colonies. It tolerates more shade than most sunflowers and produces smaller, more numerous 2-inch yellow blooms from late summer into fall. The flowers draw a wide range of bees, hoverflies, and butterflies, while goldfinches and other seed-eating birds work the ripening heads through autumn. Divide crowded clumps every few years to keep vigor up and prevent overcrowding of neighboring plants.

planting.note: Surface-sow the fine seed in fall or early spring on well-drained prairie or savanna soil, pressing it in without covering since light aids germination.

directions: Surface-sow the fine seed in fall or early spring on well-drained prairie or savanna soil, pressing it in without covering since light aids germination. This basal-rosette species sends up branched clusters of small daisy-like yellow flowers in late spring, well ahead of most tallgrass prairie bloomers, making it an important early-season nectar and pollen source for small bees and emerging butterflies. It self-sows modestly and naturalizes well in dry, sandy or gravelly prairie restorations without becoming aggressive. Leave the winter rosettes undisturbed, as they are evergreen and provide early cover in the off-season.

planting.note: Sow seed outdoors in fall so winter cold breaks dormancy naturally; established plants resent transplanting once their taproot forms.

directions: Sow seed outdoors in fall so winter cold breaks dormancy naturally, or refrigerate moist seed before spring sowing; established plants resent transplanting once their taproot forms. This upright, late-summer-blooming larkspur sends up narrow spikes of deep blue-violet flowers that are a favorite of long-tongued bumblebees and are visited by hummingbirds as well. It is native to open woodlands, rocky slopes, and prairie-woodland transitions of the Appalachians and lower Midwest, and appreciates a lean, well-drained soil rather than rich garden loam. Because it is regionally uncommon in the wild, garden-grown stock helps take pressure off native populations while still supplying valuable late-season forage.

planting.note: Press seed lightly into bare, well-drained soil in spring, or plant rooted stolon offsets for faster establishment.

directions: Press seed lightly into bare, well-drained soil in spring, or plant rooted stolon offsets for faster establishment on dry lawns, prairies, or rocky openings. Silvery basal foliage forms a dense mat that spreads by runners into a durable low groundcover, topped in mid-spring by clusters of small whitish-pink flowers on separate male and female plants. It is the primary larval host for the American Lady butterfly and offers early pollen to small native bees at a time when few other flowers are open. Once established it needs almost no supplemental water or fertilizer and tolerates foot traffic and poor soil better than turfgrass.

planting.note: Sow stratified seed on the soil surface in fall since it needs light and winter chilling to germinate; be patient, plants typically take two to three years to reach flowering size.

directions: Sow stratified seed on the soil surface in fall since it needs light and winter chilling to germinate, and be patient — plants typically take two to three years to reach flowering size. Clusters of creamy-yellow, bottle-shaped flowers open in late summer at the stem tips of this upland prairie and woodland-edge species, and they are almost exclusively pollinated by large bumblebees strong enough to force the petals apart. Plant it in a mesic to dry-mesic prairie planting or oak savanna restoration where it will not be shaded out or overtopped by aggressive neighbors. Once established the deep-rooted crown is long-lived and rewards minimal disturbance.
